archetype.name: Dual-Threat (aggressive downfield)
archetype.definition: A big-armed passer who wins with intermediate and deep throws he is willing to force, then finishes drives himself as the offense's goal-line runner.

report.headline: The deep ball and his legs drive the season; the picks come with them.
report.take:
Josh Allen in 2026 is the same player he has been for most of a decade, playing more aggressively. His 0.191 EPA per dropback ranks 8th of 54 and sits 0.212 above the qualifier average. His 8.65 yards per attempt ranks 7th. The completion rate fell from 69.3% last year to 65%, while yards per attempt rose by 0.68. That is the trade he made: aggressiveness up 2.7 points to 14.01%, and intended air yards of 9.06 against a 7.1 aDOT last season. He is throwing into tighter windows and further downfield, and it is paying off.

The passing value sits almost entirely at 10+ air yards. Those 96 throws added 46.5 EPA at 0.484 a play, with 10 touchdowns and a 7.8 CPOE. Everything underneath added 22.6 EPA at 0.14. The deep shots alone, 42 of them, produced 27.7 EPA, 7 touchdowns and 5 interceptions. His fantasy line rests on something passing totals don't show: 11 rushing touchdowns, 9 of them on designed runs averaging 2.53 yards a carry. Buffalo uses him as its short-yardage and goal-line back. That covers for a red-zone passing game that has been poor: a 43.9% completion rate and -12.4 CPOE inside the 20.

The numbers hide two things. First, the volume is modest by design. Buffalo's pass rate over expected is -5.4, 27th in the league, and he averages only 28.6 attempts. The 247 yards a game come from efficiency, not volume. Second, the interceptions are part of the profile, not a slump. Seven picks rank 44th of 54, and six of them came on 10+ air-yard throws. His career shows the same pattern: 18 picks in 2023, 15 in 2021, 10 last year. He accepts turnovers as the cost of explosive plays, and the explosive plays have more than paid for them.

The last three games show a dip. EPA per dropback fell to 0.108 and CPOE to -2.7. That stretch included the league's top-ranked defense (Minnesota) and two comfortable wins where Buffalo leaned on the run. Over the last five games he is essentially at his season line. His pressure-to-sack rate has recovered from 40.4% last year (47th) to 30.4%, closer to his normal range. That is a real repair, not noise.

strengths.title: Downfield throws carry the offense
strengths.body: His throws of 20+ air yards return 0.659 EPA a play with an 8.0 CPOE, so he is completing difficult deep balls at a rate above expectation, not just hoping. This comes from arm talent plus a deliberate jump in aggressiveness this year. The interceptions will keep coming, but the volume of big plays is sustainable because it matches his 2020-2024 peak profile.

strengths.title: Goal-line runner and scramble value
strengths.body: Nine designed-run touchdowns and a 69.4% success rate on designed runs make him the Bills' short-yardage hammer. His 20 scrambles average 0.955 EPA and moved the chains 13 times, which pays for the hits he takes extending plays. The role is stable. Eleven rushing touchdowns in nine games is an extreme rate that should cool, but not disappear.

strengths.title: Pocket management repaired
strengths.body: His pressure-to-sack rate fell from 40.4% last season (47th) to 30.4% this year. His bad-throw rate ranks 9th of 42. The 6.5% sack rate beats the league average, so the sack problem from last year looks like the blip, not the new normal.

concerns.title: Interceptions ride with the aggression
concerns.body: Seven picks rank 44th of 54, five of them on deep throws. This is the price of the downfield approach and a career-long trait, not a new flaw. Expect roughly one pick most weeks. The costly version is when it lands in a close game, though so far his within-one-score EPA has held up.

concerns.title: Red-zone passing is broken
concerns.body: Inside the 20 he completes 43.9% with a -12.4 CPOE and negative EPA. Part of this is structural: the Bills hand him the ball on designed runs near the goal line, which leaves harder, condensed-field throws. If the rushing touchdowns cool, this weakness becomes more visible in his scoring.

concerns.title: Recent accuracy and rushing dip
concerns.body: Over the last three games his CPOE is 4.8 points below his season mark and his rushing yards are down 15.6 a game. The schedule (Minnesota, ranked 1st) and comfortable leads explain much of it. Still, an 11-of-21 day against the 30th-ranked Jets defense is worth monitoring rather than dismissing.

trend.note: Single games swing widely, from 12.7 passing EPA against Detroit to 0.2 at Minnesota. His last five games sit almost exactly on his season rates. The last three show softer efficiency, which tracks with a tough defense and blowout scripts more than with decline.

nextGame.headline: A leaky Miami pass defense, if Buffalo bothers to throw
nextGame.body:
Miami's defense is built to give up exactly what Allen does best. It ranks 27th in pass EPA allowed, 26th on deep throws at 0.74 EPA a play, and 27th in sack rate. It allows 2.11 quarterback touchdowns a game (28th). Its tight-end coverage is the worst in the league by EPA, which sets up Dalton Kincaid, Allen's most efficient target. The catch is game script. Buffalo is a 16.5-point favorite already leaning run-heavy, and Miami holds quarterbacks to just 218 yards a game (3rd fewest). Expect efficiency and touchdowns more than volume, with the goal-line runs doing a lot of the scoring.

Buffalo's offense arrives intact; the only listed injury is a receiver who hasn't played. Miami is short on the interior defensive line: Zeek Biggers is out for the season and Jordan Phillips is questionable, which thins the push in his face and helps the run game. Miami is also without quarterback Malik Willis and center Aaron Brewer. That weakens its offense and raises the odds of an early Bills lead and a quiet fourth quarter for Allen. The early forecast shows gusts near 27 mph at an outdoor stadium. It is too far out to bank on, but sustained wind would take some air out of the deep shots.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots vs Miami's weak secondary
keyMatchups.body: Allen's 20+ yard throws produce 0.659 EPA a play, and Miami allows 0.74 EPA on deep passes, 26th in the league. That is the cleanest edge in the game, and it only needs a handful of attempts to swing his day.

keyMatchups.title: Kincaid against the worst TE defense
keyMatchups.body: Miami ranks 32nd in EPA allowed to opposing lead tight ends. Kincaid already leads Allen's targets in EPA per target, so the middle of the field should be open.

keyMatchups.title: Blowout script caps the volume
keyMatchups.body: A 16.5-point spread against a Miami offense ranked 25th in EPA points to an early lead. Buffalo's run-leaning tendency would then trim Allen's attempts and second-half snaps, as in recent wins over Baltimore and the Jets.

nextGame.watch: How many first-half deep shots he takes before the lead lets Buffalo turn to the run, and whether the wind cooperates.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is durable. His downfield efficiency matches his best seasons, the sack rate has normalized, and the offense ranks 3rd in EPA with his targets healthy. Expect passing efficiency to settle near his season level, roughly 225-265 yards a game on modest attempts, because the Bills will keep running when ahead. The interceptions won't go away either; roughly one a game is his baseline when he plays this aggressively.

The number most likely to regress is the rushing touchdowns. The goal-line role is real, but eleven through nine games is a rate few quarterbacks sustain. Some of those scores should shift back to his arm, which would also ease the ugly red-zone passing numbers. Fantasy output should drift from the mid-20s toward roughly 19-25 points a game, still near the top of the position.
swingFactors: How often blowout leads cut his attempts
Whether the deep-ball hit rate holds

confidence.note: Nine games fit an eight-year profile, but the TD splits and game script swing week to week.
